sourceEvidence.label: RIVT object-storage incident and source evidence
sourceEvidence.driftNote: The incident document and unrelated structured-logger files moved in the working tree while source architecture was inspected at the target revision.

assessment.summary: RIVT can centralize application-owned object authority behind one gateway and reuse its existing append-only audit ledger; this is proposed, not implemented, and provider-level access evidence remains a separate higher-cost option.

nonNegotiables: Do not claim a signed-link issuance proves a download.
Do not store object keys, signed URLs, filenames, content, credentials, authorization headers, provider errors, or raw IP addresses in application audit events.
Do not add a new audit table for the recommended option.
Do not create a service, bucket, migration, provider setting, or paid resource without separate review and owner approval.
Preserve existing authorization and the append-only audit_events trigger.
assumptions: No measured storage-route latency or database-write budget was supplied.
No provider-level immutable logging capability, retention design, or price has been verified.
Application-level actor and issuance evidence is the immediate control objective.
Historical access that was never recorded cannot be reconstructed by the proposed design.

opportunities.title: Establish accountable object-storage access
opportunities.summary: Make application object operations auditable through one owned boundary while preserving a separate decision for provider-level forensic evidence.
opportunities.diagnosis: RIVT has an append-only audit ledger, but direct S3 commands and signed-link issuance are distributed across feature modules, so object-audit coverage is convention-based and out-of-band access remains invisible.

evidence.claim: The incident records no identified misuse but cannot establish historical per-object access or prove no exfiltration.
The legacy upload schema provides stored-object records and provider object keys.
audit_events already records request, actor, organization, action, subject, timestamp, and metadata, and rejects update and delete through a trigger.
Integration coverage exercises the append-only audit_events trigger.
The shared client and signing helper coexist with direct project-media writes, and a legacy mapper can return the raw object key and optional public URL.
Album photo upload and signed-link paths exercise object authority outside a dedicated gateway.
Shop Talk media upload and link paths exercise object authority outside a dedicated gateway.
Anonymous public discovery receives signed links; the subsequent browser fetch does not traverse the RIVT server.
Credential evidence, portfolio media, and avatars include independent write, link, replacement, and deletion paths.
Document logos include the normal server-side object read plus write and delete paths.
Invoice and estimate delivery calls the document-brand read path.
Message and contact-note attachments include user-initiated writes/deletes and system cleanup.
Legacy upload routes retain list, link, and write storage behavior.
Because direct SDK and signing authority is available to several modules, object-audit completeness is controlled by caller convention rather than a single enforceable boundary.

desiredInvariants: Every application-originated object PUT, server-side GET, DELETE, and signed-link issuance reaches one auditable control before success is released.
Every event uses a canonical stored-object UUID and bounded metadata that excludes provider identifiers and customer content.
Anonymous and system operations have explicit initiators.
Audit failure prevents returning a signed URL or releasing server-read bytes.
Post-mutation audit failures use deterministic safe failure and compensation or reconciliation behavior.
New server code cannot call object SDK commands or signing functions outside the selected boundary.
Application events are represented as app operation or authorization issuance evidence, never proof of a subsequent provider download.

options.title: Local per-route audit inserts
options.summary: Keep direct storage calls and add bounded audit_events inserts independently to every current route.

evidenceCoverage.rationale: Adds future app-originated evidence but cannot reconstruct history or observe provider access.
Reuses the existing append-only ledger at each route.
Extends existing immutability tests with route-specific object events.
Known project and helper paths can emit events, but direct authority remains.
Album routes gain local events.
Shop Talk routes gain local events.
Can record anonymous link issuance but not the browser fetch.
Profile object paths gain local events.
Document-brand paths gain local events.
Delivery context must be passed into the local read audit.
Messaging and cleanup paths gain local actor/system events.
Legacy routes must be locally audited or retired.

tradeoffs.assessment: Known callers gain actor-aware events, but future and missed callers can still bypass audit.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Exercise every inventoried path and recursively search for direct SDK and signing calls.

tradeoffs.assessment: Each event adds a database insert; list routes risk N+1 writes unless independently batched.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Compare p50 and p95 route latency and database statement count on representative media lists.

tradeoffs.assessment: Events require bounded values already available to each route.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Compare process RSS for large list responses before and after batched event construction.

tradeoffs.assessment: Fail-closed and compensation behavior is repeated and may diverge by route.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Inject S3 and audit database failures into each path and compare response and compensation behavior.

tradeoffs.assessment: Incident reviewers must still inspect many audit owners and distinguish migrated from forgotten paths.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Run an audit-coverage inventory and verify action taxonomy consistency across modules.

tradeoffs.assessment: Focused route changes are easy to stage and revert without a schema or provider change.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Migrate one route family, run compatibility tests, and rehearse code rollback while preserving rows.

residualRisks: Audit ownership can drift between current and future call sites.
Signed-link issuance does not prove provider access.
Provider-console, direct-credential, and maintenance access remain invisible.
Audit and S3 mutations remain non-atomic.

workPackages: Define one shared object action and metadata contract.
Add local batched inserts and fail-closed behavior to each current route.
Add route-specific privacy and failure tests.
acceptanceCriteria: Every inventoried app operation produces one bounded audit row.
No signed URL or server-read bytes are returned after required audit failure.
No disallowed identifier or content reaches audit metadata.
migrationNotes: Use only as a temporary baseline if Option 2 cannot be delivered immediately.
implementationReadiness.rollback: Revert local inserts and route error behavior; retain immutable audit rows already written.

options.title: Centralized object-storage gateway using the existing ledger
options.summary: Make one server module the only application-owned S3 and signing boundary and write bounded rows to existing audit_events without a new table.

evidenceCoverage.rationale: Provides future application operation and issuance evidence but cannot recover history or provider access.
Uses canonical database UUIDs rather than provider keys as audit subjects; non-upload object record mapping still needs design.
Reuses the existing append-only table as the central application ledger.
Extends the existing immutability contract with gateway object-event coverage.
Moves shared signing and project-media authority into one gateway and separately removes legacy raw-key/public-URL fields.
Routes album writes and links through the gateway.
Routes Shop Talk writes and links through the gateway.
Records anonymous issuance centrally but still cannot observe the browser fetch.
Routes profile object lifecycles through the gateway without copying labels or filenames.
Routes document-logo reads, writes, and deletes through central fail-closed behavior.
Carries delivery request and actor context into the gateway read.
Routes actor and system attachment lifecycles through explicit initiator context.
Legacy routes are migrated through the gateway or retired.

tradeoffs.assessment: One owned application capability boundary makes audit omission mechanically detectable and centralizes metadata privacy and failure rules.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Add a recursive security test that permits SDK commands and signing only in the gateway, then exercise all migrated paths.

tradeoffs.assessment: Each operation adds an audit database write; central batching avoids N+1 link-list inserts but measured latency is unknown.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Compare p50/p95 latency and statement count for links, lists, uploads, deletes, and document reads against an agreed threshold.

tradeoffs.assessment: The gateway retains bounded operation context and one batch of row values already represented in the response.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Compare peak RSS and batch size for representative maximum media lists.

tradeoffs.assessment: Central behavior is easier to test, but PostgreSQL audit availability becomes part of returning storage links and server-read bytes.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Inject database and provider failures, verify fail-closed reads/links, deterministic compensation, alerts, and rehearsed route rollback.

tradeoffs.assessment: One action taxonomy, boundary, metrics surface, and static enforcement rule simplify review; alerting for audit failures is still required.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Run an incident drill that traces an object UUID across request, audit event, and safe monitoring fields.

tradeoffs.assessment: Multiple feature modules need adapters and compensation tests, although no table or service migration is required.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Migrate one route family at a time, prohibit dual audit ownership, and rehearse per-family rollback.

residualRisks: Signed-link issuance does not prove a browser fetch.
Provider console, direct credentials, backups, and maintenance scripts remain outside the gateway.
A database owner can disable the append-only trigger.
S3 mutation and PostgreSQL audit insert cannot be one atomic transaction.

workPackages: Define the gateway context, four action names, initiators, scopes, and metadata allowlist.
Implement put, server-get, delete, single-link, and batched-link behavior with fail-closed release and compensation.
Migrate read and link callers, followed by writes and deletes, preserving route authorization.
Add the server-wide direct-SDK boundary test.
Retire or migrate legacy routes and remove raw object-key/public-URL response fields.
Optionally review a separate audit_events CHECK constraint migration after the gateway is stable.
acceptanceCriteria: Only the gateway owns application SDK commands and signing.
Every app-owned operation produces one bounded event using a canonical UUID.
Link and server-read responses fail closed on required audit failure.
List responses batch audit rows without N+1 writes.
All existing authorization and functional tests pass.
No new table, service, bucket, provider setting, or paid resource is introduced by the gateway.
migrationNotes: Use adapters or per-route rollout so one audit owner is active for each operation.
A later constraint is defense in depth and requires a reviewed up/down migration; it is not required for the initial gateway.
implementationReadiness.rollback: Switch a migrated route family back to the prior adapter while preserving immutable rows and recording the temporary invariant loss.

options.title: Provider or external immutable access logging
options.summary: Retain the application gateway and add provider-native or external immutable evidence for actual storage access, subject to separate privacy, retention, cost, and provider approval.

evidenceCoverage.rationale: Can improve future evidence for actual provider access, subject to verified provider coverage; cannot reconstruct the incident's missing history.
Future provider object keys should become opaque before exporting access logs; existing objects need a compatibility plan.
The application ledger remains necessary for actor and authorization context.
Application immutability tests remain necessary alongside external evidence.
The gateway covers application intent and provider logs cover actual storage access; raw legacy fields still need removal.
Album app intent and actual provider access can both be evidenced.
Shop Talk app intent and actual provider access can both be evidenced.
Anonymous issuance stays in the app ledger and the subsequent provider fetch can be separately recorded.
Profile app intent and actual provider access can both be evidenced without exporting customer labels.
Document-logo app intent and actual provider access can both be evidenced.
Delivery request context remains in the app ledger while provider records the read.
Messaging actor/system intent and actual provider access can both be evidenced.
Legacy paths still need gateway migration or retirement even when provider access is logged.

tradeoffs.assessment: Verified provider logging can cover browser and out-of-band storage access, but the external log becomes a sensitive high-value system.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Verify provider guarantees, then test signed-link, administrative, and controlled credential-based access in non-production.

tradeoffs.assessment: Asynchronous provider export should avoid an application hop, but provider buffering, retries, and query performance are unverified.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Measure object-request latency, export delay, and query latency during bounded non-production use.

tradeoffs.assessment: Provider or external systems retain buffers, indexes, and log objects outside the application process.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Obtain provider resource accounting for peak event volume and retained data.

tradeoffs.assessment: Buffered export may preserve storage availability but creates delivery lag, retry, and loss-detection concerns.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Interrupt the sink in non-production and verify buffering, retry, alerting, reconciliation, and documented loss boundaries.

tradeoffs.assessment: A new sensitive log system requires least privilege, retention, cost alerts, delivery monitoring, incident queries, and access reviews.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Complete an operational readiness review and incident retrieval drill before production enablement.

tradeoffs.assessment: Future object keys should become opaque and provider/privacy/retention settings require separate staged changes.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Test opaque-key compatibility, protected correlation, provider enablement, and rollback without locking production data.

residualRisks: Provider logging may omit or delay some access classes depending on verified guarantees.
Logs can expose identifying object-key material unless keys become opaque.
Immutable retention can conflict with deletion and privacy obligations.
External credentials and log-reader roles create a new attack surface.
The design cannot reconstruct access that predates enablement.
Recurring cost is unknown and unapproved.

affectedComponents: Object key generation and compatibility paths
Security operations, retention, access control, and cost monitoring
workPackages: Verify provider capability, event coverage, residency, immutability, retention, deletion, and export behavior.
Obtain an exact monthly cost model and owner approval.
Move future object keys to opaque identifiers and design protected correlation.
Configure a bounded non-production delivery test and least-privilege reader access.
Add delivery-lag, loss, access-review, and spending alerts.
Perform separate production change review before enablement.
acceptanceCriteria: Provider and application events have documented, non-overclaimed meanings.
Controlled signed-link and administrative access appears within an approved delay.
No signed URL, credential, customer content, or identifying filename is exported.
Retention, deletion, residency, access, and incident procedures are approved.
The owner approves the full recurring cost ceiling before production enablement.
migrationNotes: Do not enable irreversible retention or object lock during an exploratory rollout.
Complete Option 2 first so provider evidence can be correlated with application intent.
implementationReadiness.rollback: Disable future export only after an approved change; preserve or dispose of already retained evidence according to the approved retention policy, recognizing that locked data may be intentionally irreversible.

opportunities.recommendation: Select the centralized gateway under current constraints because it makes application audit ownership enforceable, reuses the existing append-only ledger, and adds no table or paid service. Revisit provider immutable logging only when actual provider-access proof is required and its privacy, retention, operational, and exact cost constraints are approved.

openQuestions: Is provider-level proof of actual object access a launch requirement or a later assurance goal?
What latency and availability thresholds apply to audit-dependent links, lists, and server reads?
Should legacy upload routes be migrated or retired?
Is S3_PUBLIC_BASE_URL absent and is the production bucket private?
Which canonical UUID should represent document logos, avatars, and other objects that may not use uploads.id directly?
How long should application object-audit rows be retained and who may query them?
If external logging is selected, which provider and sink meet required coverage, privacy, residency, deletion, immutability, and cost constraints?
How should backup and maintenance scripts be attributed without granting them ambient unaudited authority?
